# What Is Machine Learning?

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
The mathematical formulation of supervised learning and classification theory is developed in greater depth in Chapters 5 and 6 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Chapter objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to explain what machine learning is, distinguish it from traditional programming, and identify classification, regression, and clustering problems.

## Introduction

Machine learning makes it possible to build models capable of learning patterns from data.

In traditional programming, a person defines explicit rules. In machine learning, examples are provided so that an algorithm can learn a relationship between input variables and an expected output.

## Traditional programming versus machine learning

```{r traditional-programming-rule}
pm10 <- 85

if (pm10 > 75) {
  print("High pollution")
} else {
  print("Low pollution")
}
```

::: {.callout-note title="Code explanation"}
A PM10 value is defined and then a fixed rule is applied. If the value is greater than 75, the program classifies the day as having high pollution.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Result interpretation"}
This example represents traditional programming: the decision depends on a manually written rule. In machine learning, the rule is learned from examples.
:::

```{r introduction-example-data}
data <- data.frame(
  day = 1:12,
  pm10 = c(42, 88, 55, 120, 63, 95, 38, 110, 72, 130, 47, 99),
  temperature = c(25, 28, 22, 30, 24, 29, 21, 31, 27, 32, 23, 30),
  humidity = c(40, 35, 60, 30, 55, 33, 65, 29, 42, 28, 62, 34),
  class = c("Low", "High", "Low", "High", "Low", "High", "Low", "High", "Low", "High", "Low", "High")
)

data
```

::: {.callout-note title="Code explanation"}
A small data set with 12 days is created. Each row contains environmental variables and a known class.
:::

## Predictors and response variable

The response variable is the variable we want to predict. Predictors are the variables used as inputs to the model.

## Main types of machine learning

1. Supervised learning.
2. Unsupervised learning.
3. Reinforcement learning.

## Basic notation

Suppose we have $n$ observations and $p$ predictors. We can represent the data using a matrix $X$ and a response variable $Y$.

$$
\hat{y} = f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p)
$$

## First visual example in R

```{r introduction-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
library(ggplot2)
source("../util_graficas.R")

ggplot(data, aes(x = pm10, y = temperature, color = class)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.9) +
  escala_clases_color() +
  labs(
    title = "Introductory classification example",
    subtitle = "Classification of high or low pollution",
    x = "PM10",
    y = "Temperature",
    color = "Class"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Code explanation"}
The plot places PM10 on the horizontal axis and temperature on the vertical axis, and uses color to distinguish the classes. The shared plotting functions keep the graphical identity consistent with the Spanish edition.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Result interpretation"}
The points make it possible to inspect whether the classes tend to separate. This is the basic idea behind many classification methods.
:::

## Training and test split

```{r training-test-split}
set.seed(123)
n <- nrow(data)
training_indices <- sample(1:n, size = round(0.7 * n))

training <- data[training_indices, ]
test <- data[-training_indices, ]

training
test
```

::: {.callout-note title="Code explanation"}
The data set is divided into two parts: one for training the model and another for evaluating its performance on observations not used during fitting.
:::

## First rule-based classifier

```{r rule-based-classifier}
data$rule_prediction <- ifelse(data$pm10 > 75, "High", "Low")

confusion_matrix <- table(
  Actual = data$class,
  Predicted = data$rule_prediction
)

confusion_matrix
mean(data$class == data$rule_prediction)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Result interpretation"}
The confusion matrix compares the actual class with the predicted class. Accuracy measures the proportion of correct predictions.
:::

## Interactive laboratory: a classification rule

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
This laboratory shows how a simple rule can classify observations using a threshold.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 680
#| components: [viewer]

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Threshold-based classifier"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("threshold", "Classification threshold", 0, 10, 5, step = 0.1),
      sliderInput("noise", "Noise level", 0, 3, 1, step = 0.1),
      numericInput("seed", "Seed", 123, min = 1)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("plot", height = "400px"),
      tableOutput("metrics"),
      textOutput("rule")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  data_sim <- reactive({
    set.seed(input$seed)
    x <- seq(0.5, 9.5, length.out = 80)
    actual_class <- ifelse(x + rnorm(length(x), 0, input$noise) >= 5, 1, 0)
    pred <- ifelse(x >= input$threshold, 1, 0)
    data.frame(x, actual_class, pred)
  })

  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    d <- data_sim()
    plot(d$x, jitter(d$actual_class, amount = 0.08), pch = 19,
         xlab = "Predictor x", ylab = "Actual class",
         yaxt = "n", main = "Classification rule")
    axis(2, at = c(0, 1), labels = c("Class 0", "Class 1"))
    abline(v = input$threshold, lwd = 3, lty = 2)
    grid()
  })

  output$metrics <- renderTable({
    d <- data_sim()
    data.frame(
      Observations = nrow(d),
      Correct = sum(d$actual_class == d$pred),
      Errors = sum(d$actual_class != d$pred),
      Accuracy = round(mean(d$actual_class == d$pred), 4)
    )
  })

  output$rule <- renderText({
    paste0("If x >= ", round(input$threshold, 2),
           ", predict Class 1; otherwise, Class 0.")
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
### Laboratory available in the web edition
The web edition allows the reader to change the classification threshold and observe the resulting accuracy.
:::

## Conclusion

Machine learning makes it possible to build models that learn patterns from data. In this chapter we examined the difference between manually specified rules and learning from examples.
